context.hint: A local preshared-credential service is started and one object tuple is seeded through authenticated calls. The ordinary unary listing RPC rejects a request with no credential, but the streaming listing RPC returns the seeded object identifier without one. Which defect explains the asymmetry: no streaming authentication interceptor, replacement of the stream context with a fresh background context, or both?
context.surface: Go network service with an in-memory datastore, a reusable preshared-credential authenticator, unary and streaming object-listing handlers, and a disposable local service fixture.
assumptions: The observer can read and modify a disposable local source tree and run the Go toolchain; no public service, production datastore, or live target is used.
The attacker can reach both listing RPCs over the local network and can omit, corrupt, or supply credential metadata; the attacker cannot change server configuration or read the datastore directly.
A valid credential is available for the positive control, and a health RPC has an explicit unary authentication override.
Official benchmark verification is performed outside the producing container; local builds and test logs are evidence for the repair, not an official pass.

incumbent.text: Add a streaming authentication interceptor built from the same authenticator used by the unary interceptor, wire it into server startup, and make the streaming handler use the server stream context. Validate with a preshared-credential service that missing and invalid credentials are rejected on both RPCs, valid credentials succeed, and the handler retains the stream context.

candidates.text: Hypothesis: the unary authentication interceptor is the only installed boundary, and the streaming handler's fresh background context is the sole streaming defect; only context replacement needs repair. Prerequisites: local service with a reusable preshared credential, one seeded object tuple, and a server stream whose context carries a cancellable value. Bounded test: call the streaming listing RPC with no credential and a context value, and record whether the handler observes the value and returns the object. Expected supporting result: the handler sees the injected value and the streaming path can be fixed by context adoption alone. Falsifier: the streaming call still succeeds without a credential after only the context change. Cleanup: stop the service and delete the seeded store.

Hypothesis: server startup registers only a unary interceptor chain, so per-stream interceptors are absent and the streaming listing RPC bypasses the authenticator. Prerequisites: preshared-credential service, one seeded tuple, and the ability to call both RPCs without metadata. Bounded test: compare a missing-credential unary listing call with a missing-credential streaming call, recording status and returned identifiers. Expected supporting result: unary is rejected while streaming returns the seeded identifier. Falsifier: both calls are rejected or both are accepted. Cleanup: stop the service and delete the seeded store.

Hypothesis: revocation semantics differ because a stream opened with a valid credential keeps its authorization decision for the stream lifetime, while unary calls re-authenticate per request. Prerequisites: a mutable authenticator that can rotate accepted credentials without restart, a seeded tuple, and a long-lived stream. Bounded test: open a credentialed stream, rotate the credential to reject it, then continue reading objects on the same stream and issue a fresh unary call. Expected supporting result: the old stream keeps disclosing after rotation while a fresh call fails. Falsifier: the old stream fails immediately after rotation. Cleanup: restore the accepted credentials and delete the store.

Hypothesis: authorization denial leaks object existence because unary and streaming errors differ for existing versus missing objects. Prerequisites: two seeded stores, one with a known tuple and one empty, plus missing credentials. Bounded test: compare status and message shapes for existing and missing object combinations on both RPCs. Expected supporting result: the streaming denial exposes an existence-dependent message. Falsifier: all unauthenticated responses are indistinguishable. Cleanup: delete both stores.

Hypothesis: a complete repair requires both a streaming interceptor and adoption of the server stream context; either change alone leaves a separately observable defect. Prerequisites: local service harness, a fake server stream carrying a context value, and a datastore stub that records the context. Bounded test: apply only interception, then only context adoption, then both, and check authorization plus context-value propagation. Expected supporting result: both changes are needed for the full matrix. Falsifier: one change passes every check. Cleanup: restore the disposable copy.

evaluations.rationale: Selected. Directly tests the suspected wiring gap with a cheap behavioral discriminator: the same unauthenticated caller should be rejected on the unary path and accepted on the streaming path. This distinguishes a missing stream interceptor from a broken authorizer and uses only the local fixture.
Deferred. Context-only repair is plausible but incomplete unless the streaming interceptor already exists; the candidate would mainly prove that context replacement alone is insufficient.
Deferred. Strong closure plan that tests both changes independently, but premature before the baseline bypass is observed and the repair is written.
Deferred. Revocation persistence is a real but secondary property and needs a mutable authenticator plus long-lived stream fixture, making it more expensive than the initial discriminator.
Deferred. Error-shape information disclosure is secondary to the authorization bypass and requires a two-store comparison matrix.
Incumbent retained. It remains the best end-state repair, but it had not been executed when this step was selected; the winning candidate supplies the first discriminating observation.

observation.summary: Executed a fresh preshared-credential service, seeded one object tuple through authenticated calls, and compared missing-credential unary and streaming listing calls. The unary call failed with a missing-credential status, while the streaming call returned the seeded object identifier with no error; a credentialed streaming call also returned it. This supports the explanation that only a unary interceptor is installed and the streaming endpoint bypasses authentication. It also shows that the dropped stream context is not required to explain the disclosure. Local only; no official harness was run.
observation.next_hint: Apply the smallest repair that installs the same authenticator as a streaming interceptor and adopts the server stream context, then run a missing/invalid/valid credential matrix and a stream-context propagation probe.
